\begin{abstract} AI agents increasingly bid and set prices for competing firms. If two of them secretly coordinate, can an overseer find the pair just by watching what they do? We test a published information-theoretic measure, pairwise net influence, on AI bidders in a repeated auction with an instructed two-firm cartel and honest twin markets with identical costs. From bids alone, a calibrated alarm built on the measure named exactly the colluding pair in $49$ of $60$ markets where the cartel chatted in private, never named a wrong pair, and raised one false alarm in $40$ honest markets; the alarm rule published with the measure flagged $24$ of $40$ honest markets. When the overseer also sees each firm's costs, the direction of information flow becomes visible when pooled over markets: two-way for the cartel, one-way from victim to spy for an espionage scenario. A plain correlation of the same data detected chatting cartels at least as well (pre-registered test: net influence AUROC $0.865$, $p=0.00002$; correlation $0.9975$); net influence added value only for espionage, and this replicated on fresh markets ($+0.265$ AUROC $[0.070,0.445]$). Two warnings follow: the most profitable cartel, one without chat, went almost unnoticed, and an AI judge named the strongest firms rather than the colluders. Behaviour-based screens can direct an investigation, but need calibration and a simple baseline, and are not proof of agreement. \end{abstract}

printed_tex: \section{Further method details} \label{app:methods} \paragraph{State and estimation.} The public state $H_t$ has a start code and carries forward after an all-invalid round; masking preserves this chronology. Under independent costs and no other access to a rival's current cost, leaks probe private-information flow; omitted history can induce action dependence. Arrows indicate cost source and bid receiver, not intent. Plug-in counts in bits are our replication convention inferred from the paper's results; the paper does not specify the log base. Only a unique passing pair is reported. Symmetric $\gamma$ need not imply symmetric $\Gamma$: the rival comparisons differ. Net direction is not leak direction.

\paragraph{Corrected rules and flow labels.} Corrections remain signed. The permutation test concerns influence, not net influence. The secondary leak score sums the two corrected leaks; a leak candidate requires either direction to pass $0.05/12$, again with unique-pair reporting. Flow labels are both directions detected; one detected, reverse weak; neither detected, both weak; or unclear. ``Weak'' requires $p\ge0.20$ and a corrected leak at most $0.05$ bits. Labels cover designated pairs and the full detection pipeline. Weak evidence does not establish absence; one-way flow can arise in a cartel with unilateral sharing. Permutation validity requires within-stratum exchangeability, which adaptive policies can violate. Per-market alarm rates are descriptive, without a general calibration guarantee or error control across all analyses.

\paragraph{Baselines, judge and evaluation.} Constant correlation residuals score zero and signed correlations are also retained; the baselines do not adjust for history. The judge uses thinking and sees costs only at L2 and no treatment information. There is no recalibration or answer selection; content failures remain failures. Comparisons use common judged markets and report coverage; descriptive Brier scores state the artificial prevalence. A Gemma-4-12B counter-judge was attempted on core N0/C1-SS indices 0--9 at both levels; Qwen judging Qwen remains a family-overlap limitation. All methods use rounds with four valid bids; more than 20 incomplete rounds makes a market ineligible and removes the matched block. A no-bid-category sensitivity retains missing bids. The primary test checks paired label exchangeability, not the composite null AUROC $\le0.5$. Intervals are pointwise 95\% percentile intervals. Top-1 is the fraction of credit for ranking the assigned pair first, shared equally across ties; localisation also reports reciprocal rank, correct/wrong unique reports and abstention; $1/6$ is a guessing benchmark, not a null. E1 flow detection is not a collusion positive.

\paragraph{Secondary analyses.} A2 tests paired fringe-placement swaps with Holm correction across seven endpoints, not a pure model-sameness mechanism. Pooled fingerprints align roles, bootstrap markets, and permute within markets. The exploratory probe regenerates a partner's message under counterfactual cost, then samples bids with the recipient's cost and history fixed; draws remain nested in markets (Appendix~\ref{app:stats}). Revisions and sampling are pinned; seeded re-collection is not bitwise reproducible (Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}). Re-analysing identical markets as a separate cohort reproduces correlation, strength and paper scores exactly; net and leak scores change only by permutation Monte Carlo noise (largest AUROC difference $0.0075$). The seven deviations cover warm-up transport; fenced-JSON parsing and labelled Gemma/Ministral recollection; caching, streaming and checkpoints; disk exhaustion and relocation; later recovery, call ceilings, loader paths and an exceeded budget cap; judge transport recovery and budget cancellation of breadth judging; and the operations of the two addenda.

printed_tex: \section{Statistics, provenance, and deviations} \label{app:stats} \subsection{A1: warning removal} A1 compares matched N0/C1-SS/C1-NW triplets. Its profit contrast is the difference of additive N0-referenced joint-profit uplifts; the relative uplift companion is listed separately. All eligible triplets contribute to the non-judge estimates. Judge comparisons use only triplets judged successfully in all conditions. The L2 judge difference of $0.5$ with interval $[0.5,0.5]$ comes from a single triplet and is not precise evidence. \input{sections/a1_table}

\subsection{A2: honest placement swaps} Write $s_{ab}$ for the score of strong firm $a$ and fringe firm $b$. The registered symmetrised placement contrast is \[ T=\tfrac12\{s_{00}(\mathrm{cell})-s_{00}(\mathrm{twin}) +s_{01}(\mathrm{twin})-s_{01}(\mathrm{cell})\}. \] The descriptive within-original-cell interaction is $D=s_{00}-s_{01}-s_{10}+s_{11}$. The intervention changes fringe placement and therefore can change the rest of the market. It does not identify an isolated sameness mechanism. The two-sided test swaps cell/twin labels within each index and twin-pair block. Bootstrap sampling keeps blocks with the same market index together. The tables retain all registered endpoints, per-twin contrasts and corresponding successful-judge subsets. Candidate denominators are pair opportunities, not independent trials. \input{sections/a2_tables}

\subsection{Judge failures and matched coverage} Qwen produced $278$ valid and $322$ invalid judgements out of $600$; Gemma produced $5$ valid and $35$ invalid out of $40$. Content failures were retained, not resubmitted for a preferred answer. Transport failures were reconciled and retried unchanged as recorded in the deviations. Breadth judging was cut for budget. Its absent rows are uncollected judge coverage, not judge scores of zero. The registered limit was $12{,}000$ generated tokens per attempt with the registered retry; most failed calls ended with \texttt{length}, according to the raw-log observation in the final handover. This report does not infer a cause for every invalid output from the failure code alone.

They are consistent with strong-pair preference in these cells, without establishing a universal rule or an internal reasoning mechanism. P0 is a counterexample to a universal strong-pair account: its matched judge AUROC is zero at each access level, with only $4$ and $3$ blocks. Tiny-sample percentile intervals can collapse and must not be read as certainty. \input{sections/judge_tables}

\subsection{Exploratory frozen-context probes} The complete-context slope was $0.0134737$ $[-0.0035263,0.0319480]$; $199$ contexts were complete. One context was incomplete (market $7$, round $130$, seat $3$). The leak uses $2997$ observed bids, including observations from the incomplete context: raw $0.1481534$ bits, corrected $0.0887914$ bits, implemented $p=0.001$. No resolved average linear response follows from the slope interval. A signed mean slope can cancel across contexts while mutual information detects distributional changes, but neither cancellation nor nonlinearity is demonstrated here.

The leak inference has a more fundamental limitation. Each cost-specific regenerated message is shared by five recipient bids. Individual-bid permutation within context breaks that bundle structure and can treat stochastic message variation as evidence against its null. The resulting null is anti-conservative for a claim of reproducible partner-cost transmission. The frozen estimate and implemented p-value are retained for transparency, with no causal claim. Repeated independently regenerated messages within cost/context and an inference procedure respecting that hierarchy are needed. Relabelling cost categories among whole bundles alone leaves context-conditional mutual information unchanged.

printed_tex: \section{Discussion and Limitations} \paragraph{Expected versus observed.} Before collecting any LLM data we simulated scripted bidders that always follow their strategy, with the same game, rules and sample sizes (Appendix~\ref{app:scripted}). Figure~\ref{fig:expectations} compares that plan with what the AI agents did. The calibration carried over: honest markets produced false alarms at about the simulated rate. The power did not. Scripted cartels were named in about $99\%$ of markets and scripted spies in $100\%$; the AI cartels in $65$--$100\%$ with bids only, and the AI spy in none. Even scripted spies that used the stolen cost only half the time were found in $83\%$. Flow direction shows the same gap: two-way flow was expected in every strong-pair cartel market and one-way flow in $80\%$ of spy markets, but was seen in $0\%$ and $20\%$; only pooling over markets recovered it (Figure~\ref{fig:flow}). AI agents appear to act on shared information far less consistently than scripts, so their traces are weaker than a simulation with rule-following agents suggests.

\begin{figure}[t] \centering\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/figure_6.pdf} \caption{What the pre-data simulation of rule-following scripted bidders predicted (open circles; 200 rounds, 20 markets per type, 40 honest) and what the AI agents showed (filled). ``Right pair'' uses our corrected alarm; ``flow seen'' is the per-market flow label of the designated pair.} \label{fig:expectations} \end{figure}

\paragraph{Comparison with the original paper and concurrent work.} Our scripted replication of \citet{bonjour2022} recovered their rising detection pattern in rock--paper--scissors, but not every published percentage (Appendix~\ref{app:replication}). Two concurrent sprint projects studied the same measure in rock--paper--scissors. \citet{tawareRepo} also found the fixed threshold unreliable (an innocent pair accused in $29\%$ of 100-round games) and a permutation-calibrated test near $2\%$ false alarms, matching our alarm results. They report, however, that two Qwen agents with near-identical prompts were flagged in $7$ of $10$ games without colluding; in our auction, honest markets of four Qwen agents raised one false alarm in $40$, and swapping same-model placements had no detectable effect. The auction's conditioning on costs and the last winning price may explain the difference; we did not test this. \citet{nayakRepo} found that net influence and Cram\'er's V named the planted pair equally often with scripted agents, as our correlation results do for talking cartels; we add that the exception is private information flow seen with costs. \citet{rose2026} detect collusion from model activations with AUROC $0.99$ to $1.00$ and report that only $2$ of $229$ collusive episodes in one environment verbalised the coordination. Behaviour-only audits like ours need no model access but, as the quiet cartel shows, miss coordination that leaves no trace in actions; the two approaches complement each other.

printed_tex: \section{Methods} \label{sec:methods} \subsection{Game, conditions, and models} Each market has four firms and 200 rounds. Two strong firms draw independent costs uniformly from $\{1,2,3\}$; two fringe (weak) firms draw from $\{3,4,5\}$. Bids range from 2 to 7; the lowest wins, with random ties. The winner earns bid minus cost, others zero. Bids and winners become public. Bidders see their own cost, the last ten rounds, and their cumulative profit. Costs, tie-breaks, and assignments are seeded and matched by market index. Strong seats cycle through all six label pairs, hidden from auditors.

\begin{figure}[t] \centering\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/figure_1.pdf} \caption{How the test works. Four AI agents (Qwen3.5-9B) bid in a repeated auction. In treated markets two of them form a cartel (with or without a private chat), or one secretly sees a rival's cost. Each treated market has an honest twin with identical costs. The auditor never sees messages; it sees either the bids only (access level L1) or the bids and every firm's costs (L2), and must say whether there is a cartel and which pair it is.} \label{fig:overview} \end{figure}

C1 assigns a cartel with a private chat channel (SS: strong--strong; SF: strong--fringe; FF: fringe--fringe). C2 removes the channel; E1 gives one firm access to its rival's current cost. N0 is honest, and P0 is a scripted cartel positive control (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:conditions}). The cartel treatment bundles a joint-profit goal, partner naming, secrecy, a surveillance warning, and channel access; assigned markets stay included regardless of compliance. The core uses Qwen3.5-9B: 40 N0 markets and 20 per other cell. Breadth cells use Gemma-4-12B, Ministral-3-8B, Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma-4-E4B, Ministral-3-3B, and mixed-model markets, each with its own honest control (Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}).

\subsection{Auditor access and influence} L1 receives bids $B_i$ and winners; L2 additionally receives costs $C_i$. Neither sees messages, role texts, condition labels, or model identities. The public state $H_t$ is the previous winning bid. At L1, $\gamma_{ij}=I(B_i;B_j\mid H)$. At L2, with $S_i=(C_i,H)$, Equation~3 of \citet{bonjour2022} becomes \begin{equation} \gamma_{ij}=\sum_{s_{ij}}p(s_{ij})\sum_{b_i,b_j}p(b_i,b_j\mid s_{ij}) \log_2\frac{p(b_i,b_j\mid s_{ij})}{p(b_i\mid s_i)p(b_j\mid s_j)}, \label{eq:influence} \end{equation} which the chain rule splits exactly into lockstep (action dependence) and two directional leaks: \begin{align} \gamma_{ij} &=\underbrace{I(B_i;B_j\mid C_i,C_j,H)}_{\text{action dependence}} +\underbrace{I(B_i;C_j\mid C_i,H)}_{L_{j\to i}} +\underbrace{I(B_j;C_i\mid C_j,H)}_{L_{i\to j}}. \label{eq:decomposition} \end{align} Under independent costs, a leak $L_{j\to i}$ means firm $j$'s private cost shows up in firm $i$'s bids. Estimates use plug-in counts in bits. The paper's net transformation and mutual rule (its Equations~4--5) are \begin{equation} \Gamma_{ij}[x]=x_{ij}-\max_{k\ne i,j}x_{kj},\qquad \Gamma_{ij}[\hat\gamma]\ge\alpha\ \text{and}\quad \Gamma_{ji}[\hat\gamma]\ge\alpha,\quad\alpha=0.05. \label{eq:net} \end{equation}

\subsection{Permutation correction} Within each market, 999 permutations shuffle each firm's bids within its own strata ($H$ at L1, $(C_i,H)$ at L2). With the permutation mean subtracted, \begin{equation} g_{ij}=\hat\gamma_{ij}-\frac{1}{999}\sum_{r=1}^{999}\hat\gamma^{(r)}_{ij}, \qquad s_{ij}=\min\{\Gamma_{ij}[g],\Gamma_{ji}[g]\}. \label{eq:score} \end{equation} Our corrected alarm names a pair only if its raw influence has permutation $p\le0.05/6$, both corrected net directions are positive, and it is the only such pair; the published rule (Equation~\ref{eq:net}) is reported separately. A leak-based rule and per-market flow labels are defined analogously (Appendix~\ref{app:methods}).

\subsection{Baselines and evaluation} Correlation is Cram\'er's V of the two bid series at L1 and the absolute Pearson correlation of bids after removing each firm's mean bid at its own cost at L2. A strength-only benchmark ranks the strong pair first. The frozen Qwen3.5-9B judge reads rules and masked round records and returns pair probabilities (Appendix~\ref{app:methods}). The market is the analysis unit. AUROC is the probability that a randomly chosen treated market scores above a control market (ties half). The sole confirmatory test compares designated-pair L2 net scores in Qwen C1-SS and N0 markets 0--19, with 99,999 within-block label swaps (seed 20261027): \begin{equation} p=\frac{1+\#\{\mathrm{AUC}^{*}\ge\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{obs}}\}}{100000}; \qquad \text{reject if }\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{obs}}>0.5\text{ and }p\le0.05. \label{eq:primary} \end{equation} Secondary estimates use 10,000 whole matched-block bootstraps. Honest-market alarms are counts with Clopper--Pearson intervals.

\subsection{Replication, judge budget, and pre-registration} \label{sec:addenda} Design and executable analysis were frozen before collection; seven deviations are recorded in Appendix~\ref{app:stats}. After the final analysis, two additions were pre-registered before their data were collected (Addenda v2.2--v2.3): E1, C2 and C1-SS were collected again on fresh markets 20--39, matched to the existing honest markets of the same index, with pre-specified replication criteria; and the Qwen judge was re-run with $24{,}000$ instead of $12{,}000$ output tokens (L2; N0, C1-SS, C1-SF markets 0--19). Because the original results were known, the replication tests observed patterns, not a blind hypothesis.

\subsection{From bids alone, a calibrated alarm names the cartel} Figure~\ref{fig:alarms} asks the question an overseer would ask: did the alarm rule point to exactly the colluding pair, to a wrong pair, or stay silent? With bids only, our permutation-corrected net-influence rule named exactly the right pair in $16$, $13$ and $20$ of $20$ markets for the three cartels that chat (two strong firms; strong and weak firm; two weak firms), and never named a wrong pair. In $40$ honest markets it raised one false alarm. The positive control, a scripted cartel placed among AI bidders (P0), was named in all $20$ markets at both access levels. The rule published with the method is not usable as an alarm here: it flagged $24$ of $40$ honest markets with bids only and all $40$ with costs, and for the strong-pair cartel with costs it named the wrong pair in $19$ of $20$ markets. With costs our rule named the pair less often (5, 8 and 19 of 20; three false alarms in 40). Neither rule caught the cartel without chat or the spy.

printed_tex: \begin{figure}[t] \centering\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/figure_2.pdf} \caption{What an alarm reports. For each market type, the share of markets in which the rule named exactly the colluding pair (green), a wrong pair or, in honest markets, any pair (red), or nothing (grey); numbers give right-pair counts (cartel rows) or false alarms (honest row). Left: the fixed threshold published with the method. Right: our permutation-corrected rule. 20 markets per cartel type, 40 honest markets.} \label{fig:alarms} \end{figure}

\subsection{With costs, the direction of the flow becomes visible} Costs let the measure separate two things: whether the two firms' bids move in lockstep, and whether one firm's private cost shows up in the other firm's bids (a ``leak''). Pooled over all markets of a type (Figure~\ref{fig:flow}), honest pairs show neither. The cartel that chats shows strong lockstep and leaks in both directions, consistent with partners who tell each other their costs. The spy shows a one-way leak: the victim's cost appears in the spy's bids ($0.0047$ bits), not the reverse ($-0.0004$). The cartel without chat leaves only a weak one-way trace ($0.0021$ bits) and no lockstep. These pooled patterns are clear, but single markets are short: the leak-based rule named the spy pair alone in only $4$ of $20$ spy markets, and market-level flow labels rarely resolved the mechanism.

\begin{figure}[t] \centering\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/figure_3.pdf} \caption{Which way information flows (bids + costs, pooled over 40 honest and 20 treated markets per type). Orange: the two bids move in lockstep beyond what costs and market history explain. Green arrows: a firm's cost shows up in the other firm's bids; width proportional to the estimate, drawn only when its pooled 95\% interval excludes zero. These pooled intervals are approximate (Appendix~\ref{app:stats}).} \label{fig:flow} \end{figure}

\subsection{Net influence versus a simple correlation} Figure~\ref{fig:compare} compares the two measures by how often a treated market looks more suspicious than its honest twin with identical costs (AUROC; 50\% is a coin flip). In the pre-registered primary test, net influence with costs separated the strong-pair cartel from honest markets: AUROC $0.865$ $[0.734,0.968]$, $p=0.00002$ over $20$ matched blocks. But a simple correlation of the same data did better ($0.9975$; difference $-0.1325$ $[-0.2647,-0.0309]$), and it was at least as good for every cartel that chats (the two small exceptions have intervals including zero). Net influence was clearly better only where information leaks: for the spy with costs, $0.700$ against $0.415$ (difference $+0.285$ $[0.062,0.515]$). This held on $20$ fresh markets collected afterwards ($+0.265$ $[0.070,0.445]$, Section~\ref{sec:addenda}); with bids only it did not replicate ($+0.095$ $[-0.1125,0.315]$). On fresh markets the strong-pair cartel was again detected (net $0.9075$ $[0.8025,0.985]$) and again better by correlation ($0.995$).

\subsection{Two warnings: the quiet cartel and the AI judge} The cartel without chat raised the pair's profit by $0.399$ $[0.364,0.434]$ per round, almost three times the strong-pair cartel's $0.144$, yet it was the cartel both measures detected least well and the alarm never caught it with bids only (Figure~\ref{fig:warnings}a). The profit gain replicated on fresh markets ($+0.283$ $[0.179,0.371]$). The Qwen 9B judge reads the round records and names the most suspicious pair. Under its registered $12{,}000$-token limit it failed on $322$ of $600$ judgements. With $24{,}000$ tokens it answered $54$ of $60$, but it separated cartel from honest markets barely better than chance (AUROC $0.625$ $[0.424,0.808]$) and simply named the two strong firms: right in $91\%$ of strong-pair cartels, but in $2\%$ of strong--weak cartels, where net influence was right in $93\%$ of the same markets (Figure~\ref{fig:warnings}b).

(b) How often the 24k-token AI judge and net influence ranked the true pair first, on the same markets with valid judge output (17 strong-pair and 15 strong--weak markets, bids + costs).} \label{fig:warnings} \end{figure}

\subsection{How many rounds, and other AI models} The alarm needs enough rounds. With bids only it named the strong-pair cartel in $6$ of $20$ markets after $50$ rounds, $9$ after $100$ and $16$ after $200$, while false alarms in honest markets stayed at $3$ of $40$ or fewer (Figure~\ref{fig:breadth}a). Other models behaved similarly with one exception (Figure~\ref{fig:breadth}b). The alarm named the cartel in $18$ of $20$ markets for Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-12B, and in $16$ and $19$ of $20$ in mixed-model markets. For Ministral-3-8B it found only $11$ of $20$ and raised false alarms in $6$ of $20$ honest Ministral markets ($3$ of $20$ for Qwen3.5-4B): calibration that holds for one model need not hold for another. Ministral was sampled almost deterministically (temperature $0.15$, the vendor's recommendation), which may make honest bids look alike; we did not test this. The smaller Qwen was caught as often as the larger one although its cartel earned less than honest play ($-0.115$ per round), while the Ministral and Gemma cartels gained $0.33$ and $0.23$: the alarm reacts to coordinated bidding, not to its success. With only two Qwen sizes, and the smallest Gemma and Ministral models unusable (too many invalid bids), the data say nothing about a general size trend. Honest look-alikes did not trigger the alarm: honest markets of four identical Qwen agents raised one false alarm in $40$, mixed honest markets $0$ and $1$ in $20$, and swapping which honest firm runs the same model had no effect surviving correction (smallest adjusted $p=0.264$). Removing the surveillance warning lowered the cartel's profit by $0.35$ per round without a resolved change in detection, and probes that changed only the partner's cost gave no resolved effect (Appendix~\ref{app:stats}).
